cim: Seven global firms pledge $2B investment in South Korea
cim_eredeti: Seven global firms pledge $2B investment in South Korea
szoveg_eredeti:
Nov. 4 (Asia Today) -- Seven multinational companies reported plans to invest a combined $2 billion in South Korea's artificial intelligence data centers, semiconductor industry and renewable energy sector, the government said Wednesday.

Of the total, $1.97 billion is expected to be directed to regions outside the greater Seoul metropolitan area, supporting the government's efforts to promote balanced regional development and integrate artificial intelligence into manufacturing.

The announcement comes as investment in advanced manufacturing and data infrastructure expands alongside the development of physical AI, which combines artificial intelligence with robots and other machines operating in real-world environments.

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said the investment declarations were made during the opening of the Invest Korea Summit 2026 at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas hotel.

The total represents the largest amount of investment declarations recorded at the annual summit.

Participating companies include Britain's Nscale, France's Air Liquide, U.S.-based Amkor Technology, Singapore's Gurin Energy, Norway's Deep Wind Offshore, Japan's Tokyo Electron and Germany's Henkel.

Nscale plans to invest in AI data centers, while Amkor Technology will focus on semiconductor packaging and testing.

Tokyo Electron's investment will target semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

Air Liquide and Henkel will participate in projects involving semiconductor gases and advanced materials.

Gurin Energy and Deep Wind Offshore will invest in renewable energy, including solar and wind power.

Regional development and artificial intelligence are the two central themes of this year's summit.

The South Korean government plans to expand foreign investment through its "Five Growth Hubs and Three Special Regions" strategy, which aims to develop industries tailored to different regions.

The initiative also focuses on three major industrial projects: semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers.

Park Jung-sung, South Korea's chief trade negotiator, said the government would link foreign investment to the AI transformation of manufacturing and regional development.

"We will write a new chapter in South Korea's growth by adding foreign investment to the AI transformation of manufacturing and the Five Growth Hubs and Three Special Regions strategy," Park said in his welcoming remarks.

He outlined a series of proposed measures, including the establishment of manufacturing AI clusters and industrial complexes powered by renewable energy.

The government also plans to introduce special economic zones covering broader regions to provide regulatory exemptions and support for administrative approvals.

Additional measures include recruitment events and job fairs to help foreign-invested companies secure workers in regional areas, along with special subsidies to encourage large-scale regional investment.

The government intends to connect its industrial transformation program with foreign investment by upgrading production facilities across the country into AI-powered factories.

Industrial complexes will also be developed as centers for technology testing and commercialization.

Three additional research and development centers operated by foreign-invested companies received official designations at the summit.

The centers belong to Britain's Edwards, which manufactures vacuum pumps for semiconductor production, France's Valeo, an automotive components supplier involved in autonomous driving technology, and Japan's Ibiden, which produces graphite materials for the semiconductor industry.

All three centers are located outside the Seoul metropolitan area.

The government also plans to support investment hubs, expand regulatory flexibility and assist companies with permitting procedures.

A special subsidy program for large-scale regional investments is scheduled to be introduced next year.

Foreign direct investment declarations have continued to increase.

Last year, declared foreign direct investment exceeded $36 billion, reaching a record high.

During the first three quarters of this year, declarations totaled $22.9 billion, an increase of 10.8% from the same period a year earlier.

Conference participants also highlighted physical AI as an emerging driver of industrial competitiveness.

Lee Joon-ho, an executive vice president at LG CNS responsible for smart logistics operations, said physical AI could reshape competition in manufacturing and logistics.

"Until now, AI has answered questions, generated information and performed reasoning," Lee said. "Physical AI goes one step further."

He emphasized that combining AI with robotics could improve productivity in manufacturing and logistics beyond the automation of simple repetitive tasks.

Lee predicted that physical AI would increasingly be deployed in industrial operations involving repetitive, physically demanding or dangerous work.

He identified data and software as key factors determining competitiveness in physical AI.

Other speakers said that as robotic hardware becomes increasingly standardized, the ability to train AI using industry-specific data and integrate software with actual operations would become more important.

-- Reported by Asia Today; translated by UPI
